title: Why Being Poor Is So Expensive
sources: Wells Fargo, Overdraft Services (wellsfargo.com/checking/overdraft-services): $35 overdraft fee per item, max 3 per business day; Chase standard overdraft fee $34-35 (chase.com fee schedule)
Bankrate 2025 Checking Account and ATM Fee Survey (245 institutions, June-July 2025): average overdraft fee $26.77, average NSF fee $16.82, 94% of banks charge overdraft fees
CFPB Data Point: Checking Account Overdraft (July 2014): most debit card overdraft fees come from transactions of $24 or less, most repaid within 3 days; a $34 fee on a $24, 3-day loan = ~17,000% APR
Regulation E, 12 CFR 1005.17 (CFPB): banks must get your opt-in before charging overdraft fees on ATM and one-time debit card transactions
CFPB Data Spotlight (April 2024): banks with over $1B in assets collected $5.8B in overdraft/NSF fees in 2023 ($11-12B a year in 2015-2019)
FFIEC Call Report data (Schedule RI, item RIADH032), analysis by Motley Fool Money, Sept 2026: $2.96B in overdraft/NSF fees in the first six months of 2026 at 512 banks with over $1B in assets
CFPB Data Point: Frequent Overdrafters (Aug 2017): 9% of accounts (more than 10 overdrafts a year) paid 79% of all overdraft fees

Terry Pratchett, Men at Arms (Discworld, 1993): the Sam Vimes 'Boots' theory of socioeconomic unfairness ($50 boots last ten years; $10 boots, replaced again and again, cost $100 over the same ten years)

Orhun & Palazzolo, 'Frugality Is Hard to Afford', Journal of Marketing Research (2019): low-income households pay about 5.5% more per roll of toilet paper because they can't buy in bulk or stock up on sales

FTC testimony on the rent-to-own industry (July 2001): total cost of rent-to-own is usually significantly higher than retail prices; 70% of rent-to-own merchandise ends up purchased. FTC v. Progressive Leasing (2020): $175M settlement over deceptive pricing
Illustrative math: $500 TV vs $20/week x 78 weeks = $1,560 (about 3x)

CFPB, What is a payday loan? / What are the costs and fees for a payday loan?: typical two-week loan with a $15 per $100 fee = APR of almost 400%; typical $350 loan means repaying more than $400 in two weeks
Check cashing fees typically 1%-10% of the check; New York DFS cap since Jan 18, 2023: greater of $1 or 2.2% (1.5% for public assistance checks)
FDIC 2023 National Survey of Unbanked and Underbanked Households: 4.2% of U.S. households (about 5.6 million) unbanked; most cited reason: not enough money to meet minimum balance requirements

Consumer Federation of America, 'The One Hundred Percent Penalty' (July 2023): drivers with poor credit pay about twice as much for auto insurance as drivers with excellent credit and the same driving record; FTC report to Congress (2007): credit-based insurance scores predict claims; CA, HI and MA ban credit in auto insurance pricing
Bankrate, Banks that have cut or eliminated overdraft fees (Capital One, Citi and others)
Congressional Research Service IN12513 (2025): Congress repealed the CFPB's 2024 overdraft rule (which would have allowed a $5 fee)
Mullainathan & Shafir, Scarcity: Why Having Too Little Means So Much (2013)
Bank On National Account Standards 2025-2026 (CFE Fund): no overdraft or NSF fees, monthly fee $5 or less (or $10 or less if waivable), opening deposit $25 or less
NCUA Payday Alternative Loans (12 CFR 701.21(c)(7)(iii)): federal credit union PALs capped at 28% APR; CFPB, credit builder loans and secured credit cards

beats.text: Dave buys a four dollar coffee. His bank account has one dollar in it. He's three dollars short.
The card goes through anyway. Then his bank charges him a thirty five dollar overdraft fee. Total cost of that coffee: thirty nine dollars.
Now look at this. His neighbor buys the exact same coffee, with a thousand dollars in the bank. His cost? Four dollars.
Same coffee. Same shop. The only difference is how much money was already there.
That's the weird rule nobody tells you. Being poor costs extra.
Today: the hidden fees, who profits from them, and how to stop paying them.
So how did a coffee cost thirty nine dollars?
When you spend more than you have, your bank can do two things. Decline the card. Or pay it anyway, and lend you the difference. That loan is called an overdraft.
And the fee is not small. Big banks like Wells Fargo and Chase charge about thirty five dollars per overdraft. The average across banks, according to Bankrate, is about twenty seven dollars.
Here's the sneaky part. For debit cards and A T Ms, the bank needs your permission first. It's called opting in. Many people tick that box when they open the account, and forget.
The C F P B, the government's consumer watchdog, found that most debit card overdrafts are for twenty four dollars or less, and get paid back within three days.
Think about that as a loan. Borrow twenty four dollars for three days, pay a thirty four dollar fee. That's like an interest rate of seventeen thousand percent.

beats.chapter: The Raccoon at the Bottom of Your Account
beats.text: Remember the raccoon from our credit card video? He found a new job.
He sits at the bottom of your bank account, right at zero. Most people never meet him. But the second you dip below zero, toll booth.
And it adds up. The C F P B found that banks with over a billion dollars in assets collected five point eight billion dollars in overdraft and bounced payment fees in twenty twenty three.
The latest bank reports show almost three billion dollars more, in just the first six months of twenty twenty six.
But here's the shocking part. The C F P B found that just nine percent of accounts paid seventy nine percent of all overdraft fees.
So the raccoon isn't charging everyone. He's charging the same small group, over and over. The people with the least money.
This problem is so old, it even has a name. And it comes from a fantasy novel.
In nineteen ninety three, the author Terry Pratchett wrote a book called Men at Arms. His character, a city guard named Sam Vimes, explains it with boots.
A really good pair of boots costs fifty dollars. They last ten years.
A cheap pair costs ten dollars. They leak after a season or two, so you buy another pair. And another. And another.
After ten years, the rich guy spent fifty dollars on boots. The poor guy spent a hundred. And his feet are still wet.
Readers loved it so much, economists now call it the boots theory. When you can't afford the good thing, you pay more for the bad thing.
The boots theory shows up everywhere. Even in the toilet paper aisle.
A big thirty pack is cheaper per roll. But it costs twenty four dollars today. A four pack costs five dollars. If you only have ten dollars until Friday, you buy the four pack.
Researchers studied millions of shopping trips. Low income families paid about five and a half percent more per roll, because they couldn't buy big packs, or stock up during sales.
Now make it bigger. Rent to own. Dave needs a TV. The store price is five hundred dollars. He doesn't have five hundred dollars.
But the rent to own shop says: only twenty dollars a week! Seventy eight weeks later, Dave has paid one thousand five hundred sixty dollars. Three TVs for the price of one.
The Federal Trade Commission found that most rent to own customers end up buying the item. So they pay the high price in full.
Now, what happens when Dave runs out of money a week before payday?
Enter the payday loan. Borrow three hundred fifty dollars today, pay it back in two weeks, plus a fee. Usually fifteen dollars for every hundred.
Fifteen percent doesn't sound crazy. But that's for just two weeks. The C F P B says that works out to an annual rate of almost four hundred percent.
Your credit card, by comparison, charges maybe twenty five percent a year. And the C F P B found most borrowers can't pay it all back in two weeks, so they borrow again. It's a hamster wheel.
Then there's check cashing. No bank account? A check cashing store might keep anywhere from one to ten percent of your paycheck. Every single payday.
And millions of people have no bank account. The F D I C says about five point six million American households are unbanked. The number one reason? Not enough money for the minimum balance.
There's one more hidden cost. Your credit score.
Think of it as a trust meter. The lower it is, the more everyone charges you, just in case.

Car insurance is the big one. In most states, insurers can use your credit to set your price. A twenty twenty three study found drivers with poor credit paid about twice as much as drivers with excellent credit. Same car. Same clean driving record.
To be fair, insurers say credit really does predict claims, and a federal study agreed. But a few states, like California, ban it anyway.
And it doesn't stop there. No credit can mean a bigger deposit for your apartment, your electricity, and your phone. Money you need, right when you have the least.
So who's on the other side of all this? Let's follow the money.
Banks, from overdraft fees. Payday lenders, from rollovers. Rent to own stores, from weekly payments. Check cashers, from every paycheck.
Now, to be fair. Small loans cost money to make. Some people never pay them back. And an overdraft can cover rent that would otherwise bounce.
But some big banks, like Capital One and Citi, dropped overdraft fees completely, and they're still doing fine.

In twenty twenty four, the C F P B made a rule to cap overdraft fees at big banks. In twenty twenty five, Congress cancelled it. Should fees be capped? That's a political question. Now you know the numbers.

beats.chapter: Myth: They're Just Bad With Money
beats.text: Most people think poor people are poor because they're bad with money. Nope. Not that simple.
Imagine Dave and his rich neighbor make the exact same mistake. They both overspend by three dollars.
The neighbor doesn't even notice. It costs him nothing. Dave pays thirty five dollars. Same mistake. Very different price.
Remember the toilet paper study? Those families knew the big pack was a better deal. They just couldn't pay for it today.
And researchers found that money stress eats brain power. When every dollar is a puzzle, there's less room left for the long term. It's like doing homework while your house alarm is going off.

beats.chapter: How to Stop Paying the Poor Tax
beats.text: So what can you actually do? Remember, this is education, not advice.
One. Turn off overdraft on your debit card. Call your bank or check the app. Then if you're short, the card just says no. Embarrassing, but free.
Two. Look for an account with no overdraft fees at all. Search for Bank On certified accounts. No overdraft fees, and a monthly fee of five dollars or less.
Three. Turn on low balance alerts. A text when you drop under fifty dollars can save you thirty five.
Four. Build a tiny buffer. Even one hundred dollars stops most overdrafts. Call it your boots fund.

Five. Build credit slowly, with a secured card or a credit builder loan from a credit union. And if you need a small emergency loan, credit unions offer payday alternative loans, capped at twenty eight percent a year.
So let's recap.
One. Being poor costs extra. Overdrafts, payday loans and check cashing charge the most to people with the least.
Two. The boots theory. When you can't afford the good thing, or the big pack, you pay more over time.
Three. You can fight back. Turn off overdraft, find a fee free account, and build a small buffer.
Next time, Dave goes to the store for milk. Just milk. He comes out with eighty seven dollars of stuff. We'll find out why.
